title: Enzymes & Nucleic Acids Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll explore enzymes — biological catalysts — and the nucleic acids DNA and RNA.
meta_desc: A-Level Biology Biological Molecules — lock-and-key vs induced fit, Km and Vmax, inhibitors, plus DNA and RNA structure.
final_note: You learned that enzymes lower activation energy via active sites (induced fit), that Km measures affinity and Vmax measures speed, and that DNA is a double helix while RNA is single-stranded.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Enzymes are biological catalysts — they lower activation energy.

Old model: lock-and-key — fixed active site.
Modern model: induced fit — the active site moulds around the substrate, straining its bonds and speeding the reaction.

Each enzyme is highly specific because its tertiary structure gives a precise active-site shape.

Plot rate vs substrate concentration → a curve that levels at Vmax.

Km = substrate concentration giving ½ Vmax. Low Km = enzyme binds substrate strongly (high affinity).

Competitive inhibitor — binds active site → raises Km, Vmax unchanged.
Non-competitive inhibitor — binds elsewhere, distorts active site → lowers Vmax, Km unchanged.

A nucleotide = phosphate + pentose sugar + base.

DNA — double helix, deoxyribose sugar, bases A-T and C-G (3 H-bonds for C-G, 2 for A-T). Two antiparallel strands.

RNA — single-stranded, ribose sugar, uracil replaces thymine. Three types: mRNA, tRNA, rRNA.

A pairs with T (or U in RNA). C pairs with G.

options: Thymine
Uracil
Cytosine
Guanine

mcqs.q: How does a competitive inhibitor affect enzyme kinetics?
options: Lowers Vmax, Km unchanged
Raises Km, Vmax unchanged
Lowers both Km and Vmax
Raises Vmax, Km unchanged

mcqs.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
options: The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
Antibodies bind to any antigen they meet first.
The enzyme has died because enzymes are alive.
Its tertiary structure (3D shape) changes, particularly the active site, so it can no longer bind substrate effectively.

mcqs.q: Why are enzymes specific to certain substrates?
options: The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
Only substrates with complementary shape and chemistry to the active site can bind effectively.
Each enzyme can react with any substrate, but works fastest with one type.
Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.

mcqs.q: What makes the antigen-binding site of an antibody specific to one antigen?
options: Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.
The variable region — its amino acid sequence (and thus shape) differs between antibodies, complementing a specific antigen.
All antibodies have the same binding site; specificity comes from where they go in the body.
Antibodies bind to any antigen they meet first.
